one_liner: Paper-only LevelDB 1.22 fork that moves most compaction work to an NVIDIA GPU; about 2x LevelDB/RocksDB YCSB-A throughput, but only under heavy CPU contention.
what_it_does: LUDA is a research prototype from HUST that changes about 1K lines of LevelDB 1.22 and adds about 2.7K lines of CUDA 10.1 so that SST compaction runs mostly on a discrete NVIDIA GPU. Reads, writes and the memtable stay on LevelDB's normal CPU path, so the API should still be LevelDB's, though the paper never says so. Its goal is to keep writes and tail latency steady when other processes use up the host CPU. The code was never released: the paper's footnote links github.com/anonymous, which is not a real GitHub account (API returns 404).
how_it_is_fast: Compaction is split into three GPU phases that can run in parallel. An 'unpack' kernel runs per input SST, verifying each data block's CRC32 and rebuilding the prefix-compressed keys. It stores values in a KV pair buffer and emits small <key, value_offset> tuples. Packing uses three kernels: 'shared_key' rebuilds prefix-shared keys per 4 KB block, 'encode' copies values in and computes CRC32 per block, and 'filter' builds the Bloom filter block. Finished data blocks are sent back to the host with cudaMemcpyAsync while the filter is still being built. The merge-sort itself is not done on the GPU: the tuples are copied to the host, deduplicated and sorted on the CPU, then copied back (the 'cooperative sort'). Values move only twice ('lazy value movement'), and every SST goes SSD -> host RAM -> GPU and back, with no GPUDirect Storage.
when_to_use: As a design reference for moving LSM compaction CPU work (block CRC, prefix-key decode/encode, Bloom filter build) onto a GPU, on hosts where other tenants leave the KV store about 20% of the CPU. That is the only setting where it beat both baselines by about 2x.

Write-heavy or mixed (YCSB-A-shaped) workloads on very fast storage (the paper used an Intel Optane 900p), with a small host CPU (4 cores / 8 threads) and a spare NVIDIA GPU. In that setup LevelDB-style compaction is CPU-bound.

When steady 99th-percentile write latency under a LevelDB-style engine matters more than peak throughput. With no CPU stress, the paper's Fig. 12 shows LUDA with the lowest and flattest p99 of the three stores after a short warm-up spike. Under 80% CPU stress, its average write latency rose by only 7 us.

As a starting point for reading the later GPU-compaction papers that cite it (gLSM in ACM TOS 2024, RGKV in IEEE TC 2025, GPComp in TPDS 2025, gParaKV, GCLComp). gLSM's abstract adds a GPU-oriented radix sort and key-value separation, the two costs LUDA leaves on the CPU and the PCIe bus.
when_not_to_use: Whenever you need something to run. There is no source, binary, license or build instructions. GitHub searches for LUDA and for GPU LevelDB/LSM compaction find nothing, and the footnote's github.com/anonymous link is a dead placeholder.

Hosts with free CPU. With no CPU stress, stock RocksDB 6.4.6 (4 threads) finished the 5 GB YCSB-A run fastest at every value size and LUDA came second. In the one-hour 50 GB run, RocksDB with 4 background jobs also had the shortest running time.
Read-dominated workloads. LUDA does not touch the read path, and the paper blames part of its throughput loss under CPU stress on reads that get less CPU time.

Machines without an NVIDIA CUDA GPU, or where the extra PCIe traffic and host CPU cost matter. LUDA used more CPU than LevelDB because data moves back and forth between CPU and GPU, and every compaction stages SSTs in host RAM.

Workloads that need compressed SSTs or low SSD write amplification. Snappy is not implemented. Because the prototype triggers compaction only when L0 is full and does not flush the immutable memtable first, it compacts about 2x as much data as LevelDB at 128 B values.

integration.form: none published: a paper-only modification of LevelDB 1.22 (about 1K LOC changed, 2.7K LOC of CUDA added); no source, library or binary
integration.dependencies: NVIDIA GPU and CUDA toolkit 10.1 (per the paper); otherwise LevelDB 1.22's own build (CMake 3.9+, optional libsnappy, which LUDA's compaction path does not use)
integration.min_toolchain: not documented; the paper names CUDA 10.1 but no host compiler or flags. The LevelDB 1.22 base it forks sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11
integration.platforms: Tested only on x86-64 Linux (Ubuntu 16.04, kernel 4.15) with a Pascal-generation GTX 1080Ti; needs a CUDA-capable NVIDIA GPU; other GPUs, OSes and architectures not documented
integration.thread_safety: not documented; stock LevelDB's DB handle is safe for concurrent use, and the paper does not say whether the GPU compaction path changes that
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — as a LevelDB 1.22 fork it presumably keeps LevelDB's C++ API, but no code exists to check that. SSTs are written without Snappy, and on-disk compatibility with stock LevelDB files is not discussed

gotchas: The headline depends on the scenario. 'Up to 2x higher throughput' comes from the 80% stress-ng setting (20% of a 4-core CPU left) at 1 KB values. The text gives no numbers for the other cells, and Fig. 7/8 bars carry no value labels.

The '2x data processing speed' / 'compaction speed 1x faster than LevelDB' claim divides compaction bytes by running time. Part of those bytes is extra work the prototype creates for itself: it compacts about 2x LevelDB's data at 128 B values. The '46% less running time' at 1 KB does not say which CPU-stress level it refers to.

The compression settings may favor LUDA. All stores ran with 'default parameters', and LevelDB 1.22's default is kSnappyCompression whenever it is built with libsnappy, but LUDA does no compression at all. The paper does not say whether the baselines were built with Snappy, so their CPU budget may include compression work that LUDA skips.

The manuscript has draft errors. The 50 GB run is called '0.1 billion' pairs in Section IV-A but '0.1 million' in IV-D. The text cites Fig. 9 (latency) for running times that are in Fig. 8. It is an arXiv v1 (7 Apr 2020) only, with no peer-reviewed version in Crossref.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: You can't pick it for deployment, because there is no code. For a code-available LevelDB-lineage speedup, use HyperLevelDB (about 3.4x LevelDB on 100M writes). To cut compaction work itself, use PebblesDB (guards) or MatrixKV/SpanDB on fast storage. Read LUDA only as the catalogued reference for offloading compaction to a GPU when the host CPU is contended.
verified_claims_summary: The HUST authors ran YCSB-A (50/50 update/read) with 16 B keys and 128 B-1 KB values: 10M pairs loaded (about 5 GB), then 10M operations, with 4 MB memtables/SSTs, 4 KB blocks and 10-bit Bloom filters. They compared against LevelDB 1.22 and RocksDB 6.4.6 (4 threads), on a 4-core/8-thread Xeon E5-1620 v4 with 64 GB RAM, a GTX 1080Ti, an Optane 900p and Ubuntu 16.04 with CUDA 10.1, and used stress-ng to load the CPU to 0/40/80%. At 80% stress and 1 KB values, LUDA got about 2x the throughput of both baselines: RocksDB kept about 30% of its unstressed throughput and LUDA/LevelDB about 70%, and running time grew by 100 s for LUDA vs 203 s for LevelDB. With a free CPU, RocksDB was fastest. Host compiler and flags are not stated, and nobody else has reproduced the results.
status_note: Paper only: arXiv v1 (April 2020) with no later version, no journal reference and no public repository or license, so maintenance is unknown and it is usable only as a design reference. Semantic Scholar lists about 21 citing papers, including newer GPU-compaction systems (gLSM, RGKV, GPComp) that are better starting points today.
